Chapter 9: Making Messages Stick—Repetition, Anchoring, and Call to Action
You know, even the most engaging message can slip away if it’s not reinforced. So, how do you make sure your key ideas aren’t just heard—but actually remembered and acted on?
One tried-and-true tool is repetition. Think about your favorite song—the chorus sticks because you hear it over and over, right? In the same way, great communicators weave their main points throughout a conversation or presentation. But here’s the trick: it’s not about being repetitive or boring. It’s about finding creative ways to circle back to your core message, so it really lands.
Another powerful approach is anchoring. Anchoring means connecting new information to something your audience already knows—or feels strongly about. For example, imagine a health educator who talks about the benefits of exercise by linking it to the happiness of playing with your grandkids. Suddenly, the message becomes way more personal and memorable.
And don’t forget: a clear call to action is essential. People want to know, “What should I do next?” Whether it’s changing a habit, making a big decision, or just reflecting on a new idea, you need to guide them toward that next step.
So, how can you make your message stick? Try these strategies:
First, repeat your key points at just the right moments—mixing up your words and using fresh examples each time.
Second, anchor your ideas to things your audience already values, understands, or feels emotionally connected to.
And finally, always wrap up with a clear, actionable next step or an invitation to get involved.
Picture this: a nonprofit leader finishes a talk by inviting everyone to volunteer at an upcoming event. Suddenly, the message isn’t just a nice idea—it’s a call to meaningful action.
By blending repetition, anchoring, and a strong call to action, you make sure your message sticks—and that it actually matters long after the conversation is over.
